stem: A support agent has run for 60 turns. The MLflow trace shows the message history growing every turn, with old tool outputs and greetings still in the prompt. The agent now ignores the customer's latest constraint and repeats steps it finished earlier. Which technique addresses this failure most directly?

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the agent varies its steps instead of repeating the ones it has already done
Move to a model with a larger context window and keep the full history unchanged, so nothing has to be removed from the prompt
Delete every message older than the last five turns, since earlier turns rarely matter once the conversation has moved on
Compact the older turns into a short state note holding decisions, open items and constraints, and keep the latest turns verbatim

stem: A sales assistant calls a Unity Catalog SQL function, `get_orders`, that returns every column of every order for a customer. The trace shows that call as the largest span, and later answers cite the wrong order because the useful rows are lost in the output. Which change addresses the cause?

choices.text: Change the function to take a date range and a row limit and return only the columns the answer needs
Replace the SQL function with a Python function that returns the same full rows, because Python results are summarized automatically
Ask the model in the system prompt to "ignore irrelevant order columns" while leaving the function output unchanged
Cache the full function output in the session so the model does not have to call the function a second time

stem: A personal-assistant agent re-asks every user for their preferred report format and time zone in each new conversation. Raw transcripts of past chats are kept in a session store. Which two changes best fit the failure? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Keep the preferences only in the in-context conversation history of the current conversation and its prompt
Keep the memories scoped to the user they describe, so recall returns that user's preferences and no one else's
Delete the session store, because a session is the only place where memory can be kept between chats
Paste every past transcript of the user into the system prompt at the start of each new conversation
Store the stable preferences as durable facts in an agent memory store, and let the agent recall them by semantic search when relevant

stem: A research agent browses many web pages in the same context as its planning notes. After a few searches, the trace shows tens of thousands of tokens of raw page text, and the plan itself is no longer being followed. The team wants to keep the planner's context clean. Which technique fits best?

choices.text: Let the planner keep all raw pages and add an instruction to focus on the plan and skip unrelated text
Reduce the number of searches to one per run, so the planner never has to read more than a single page
Hand each search to a sub-agent with its own context, which returns only a short, sourced summary
Store each raw page in the planner's notes under a title, so that the planner can scroll back to any page

stem: A customer-service agent has this in its prompt: a rule "keep every answer under two sentences" and, further down, a rule "always list the full policy clause, the date and the exception rules". Traces show answers that are sometimes short and sometimes long for the same request. Which fix targets the cause?

choices.text: Add a third rule saying "when in doubt, follow the most recent instruction" and leave both existing rules in place
Add several few-shot examples of long answers, so the model sees that the longer rule is the one that usually applies
Rewrite the two rules into one instruction that states which wins and when, with a single answer format
Raise the maximum output tokens so the longer rule can always be satisfied without being cut off

stem: A code-migration agent writes a 12-item plan at the start of a run. After about 40 tool calls the trace shows the plan far back in the prompt, below pages of tool output, and the agent starts skipping items and declaring the job done early. Which technique targets this failure?

choices.text: Keep a short task list that the agent updates each step, and place the current list at the end of the context
Delete all tool outputs after each call so the plan is the only thing left, and the agent has no results to build on
Raise the maximum number of steps in the run, so the agent has more chances to come back to the skipped items
Repeat the original plan at the very top of the prompt a second time, so the model sees it twice before the tool outputs

stem: A log-analysis agent must answer questions about incident reports stored in Unity Catalog volumes. Loading every report into the prompt would fill the window before the first question. Which proactive strategy reduces context pressure while keeping every report reachable?

choices.text: Summarize every report once into a single paragraph and keep only those paragraphs, discarding the original files
Keep an index of report IDs and titles in context, plus a tool that loads one report when details are needed
Split each report into sentences and load all sentences in random order, so no single report takes up much space
Load the five newest reports at the start of every run, as recent incidents are likeliest to be asked

stem: An analytics agent has 28 tools, and every model call includes all their definitions. Its SQL tool also returns whole result sets. The team wants proactive measures before quality drops. Which two apply? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Expose all 28 tools at every step, because the model needs to see the full list to decide when none apply
Merge all 28 tools into one tool with a long free-text parameter that accepts any request
Pass SQL result sets unchanged so that the model sees every row, then ask it to pick the relevant ones
Give each task only the few tools it needs, instead of the full set of 28
Scope tool results: aggregate in SQL or limit rows and columns so the tool returns only what the question needs

stem: A team registers an external MCP server in the workspace so its agent can use it. The server exposes many tools, but this agent's job needs only three of them. Governance lets the team share access and restrict which tools are available. Which choice best reduces context pressure?

choices.text: Restrict the registered server to the three tools the agent needs, so only those definitions reach the model
Disable tool calling and let the agent describe what it would have called, to be run by hand afterwards
Register the server separately once for every tool, so the agent loads each tool definition one at a time
Leave all tools available, and add a system-prompt line telling the agent which three to use and to skip the rest

stem: An agent with Databricks agent memory has accumulated hundreds of stored facts about one user. The current design injects all of them into the system prompt at the start of every conversation, and latency and costs have risen. Which strategy fits best?

choices.text: Keep injecting all memories but sort them alphabetically so the model can find the one it needs more quickly
Retrieve by semantic search only the few memories relevant to the current request and add those to the context
Move all the memories into the conversation history, so they are summarized together with the chat turns
Truncate the stored memories to the first sentence of each, and inject all of them at the start as before

stem: A documentation agent has an AI Search retriever tool. Its trace shows the agent calling the retriever on every turn, including greetings and arithmetic questions, and adding five chunks each time. What is the best proactive change to the tool's configuration?

choices.text: Increase the number of chunks returned, so each call is more likely to contain something the agent can use
Remove the tool description entirely, so the model stops associating the tool with documentation questions
Write a tool description that says when to search (product documentation questions) and when not to
Set the retriever to run before every model call, so the cost of searching is paid in a single predictable place

stem: A finance agent trace shows: step 3, a tool returns "Q3 revenue: 4.2M" from a stale cache of last year's data; steps 5, 7 and 9, the agent's reasoning cites "revenue is 4.2M" as an established fact, and the final report is wrong even though a later tool call returned the correct 6.1M. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context clash, because two sources were retrieved from different vendors and the agent chose the cheaper one
Context distraction, because the context grew long enough that the agent over-weights its accumulated history over the task
Context confusion, because too many unrelated tools were defined and the agent chose the wrong source
Context poisoning, because an incorrect value entered the context and was then reused as if it were true

stem: A data-migration agent has been running for several hours. Its trace shows a very large message history in which every statement is accurate and consistent. In recent steps the agent keeps repeating actions it completed in the first hour and has stopped working on the current subtask. Which context failure explains this best?

choices.text: Context clash, because first-hour instructions contradict the instructions of the current subtask
Context poisoning, because an inaccurate statement from the first hour was reused in the plan
Context confusion, because the agent has too many near-identical tools and keeps choosing the wrong one
Context distraction, because the long history pulls the agent toward repeating past actions

stem: A helpdesk agent was given 45 tools, including `create_ticket`, `create_ticket_draft`, `update_ticket` and `log_ticket_note`, with near-identical descriptions. In the trace, when asked only to draft a ticket for review, the agent calls `create_ticket`, which files it right away. All the tool results were correct. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context confusion, because overlapping, superfluous tool definitions steered the model to the wrong tool
Context clash, because the user's request contradicts the system prompt about whether tickets may be filed
Context poisoning, because an earlier tool result put a false fact into the history
Context distraction, because the conversation is long enough that the agent forgets what it was asked to do

stem: A policy-answering agent retrieves two documents for one question: a 2023 handbook that says refunds are allowed within 30 days, and a 2025 handbook that says 14 days. In the trace, the final answer says 30 days in one sentence and 14 days in the next. Which context failure does this show?

choices.text: Context poisoning, because the 2025 handbook is a hallucination that the agent repeated several times
Context clash, because two retrieved sources contradict each other and the model has no rule for which wins
Context confusion, because the retriever returned too many tools for the agent to choose between
Context distraction, because the retrieved text is so long that the agent loses track of the question asked

stem: A planning assistant has agent memory. One day it hallucinated "the user's budget is 50k" during a chat, and a memory pipeline distilled that into a stored memory. Over the next weeks, in separate conversations, the agent keeps proposing 50k plans and cites the stored memory. Which diagnosis and remedy fit best?

choices.text: Context distraction; shorten the system prompt so that the stored memories take a smaller share of the window
Context clash; add an instruction telling the agent to prefer its own opinion over stored memories
Context poisoning that persists in memory; correct or delete the bad memory and validate what the pipeline writes
Context confusion; remove tools from the agent until it only answers budget questions

stem: A team is building a customer agent with these needs: the conversation must resume after the agent restarts, and the agent should remember each customer's preferences in later conversations. Which Databricks capability supplies this state?

choices.text: A Genie Agent that stores the conversation as sample questions for future users
Agent sessions and agent memory, both managed stores backed by Lakebase
MLflow Tracing, by replaying each stored trace as the agent's memory of the customer
Unity Catalog tags on the customer table, which the agent reads at the start of each conversation

stem: A team registers an MCP server in the workspace for several agents. Security needs to decide which groups may use it, to manage the credentials it needs, and to monitor how it is used. Which Databricks capability covers this?

choices.text: MLflow Tracing, by granting each group access to the spans that the server's tool calls produce
Lakebase, by storing the credentials and a usage log for the server in a Postgres table the agents read
AI Search, by indexing the server's tool descriptions so that only authorized groups can retrieve them
Unity Gateway, which controls access, manages credentials and monitors usage for registered MCP servers

stem: A platform team wrote a Python function that checks an order's refund eligibility. Several agents should call it as a tool, and only members of the support group may run it. Where should the function live?

choices.text: In Unity Catalog as a function, with EXECUTE granted to the support group
Inside each agent's prompt as a code block, so the model can rewrite it per request
In a Lakebase table named after the function, with a row per call to hold the result
In an MLflow experiment as a logged artifact that each agent downloads at start-up

stem: A deployed agent costs more per request and responds slower than during testing. The team wants to see, for each step of a request (model call, retriever, tool), the inputs, outputs, latency and token usage to find the step to fix. Which Databricks capability gives this view?

choices.text: Unity Catalog lineage, which shows which tables and functions the agent touched during a request
AI Search, by indexing the agent's logs and querying them by semantic similarity
MLflow Tracing, which records inputs, outputs, latency, token usage and cost of every intermediate step
Lakebase, by logging each request to a Postgres table through a custom tool call

stem: An architect compares MCP options for an agent in a Databricks workspace. Which two statements are accurate? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The Databricks SQL MCP server is recommended for open-ended natural-language business questions, because it hides SQL from the agent
Databricks-provided MCPs ignore Unity Catalog permissions, so access is controlled only in the agent's own code
The Genie Agent MCP is the right choice for any question across the whole workspace, and its calls are governed by Unity Gateway policies

The Genie One MCP server is the recommended choice for natural-language analytics across the workspace, and it is governed through Unity Gateway grants and policies plus the underlying resource permissions
A Genie Agent MCP is scoped to one curated Genie Agent, using its tables, instructions and examples, and its calls bypass Unity Gateway governance

stem: A classification agent's prompt carries 30 few-shot examples, most near-copies of each other covering the same two easy categories. The trace shows the examples are 70 percent of the prompt tokens, and the rare categories are still misclassified. Which change improves focus?

choices.text: Keep the 30 examples but repeat the category list after each one, so the categories stay in front of the model
Replace them with a handful of diverse, canonical examples that include the rare categories, and drop the near-copies
Move all 30 examples into the system prompt, so the model treats them as rules instead of examples
Add 30 more examples of the rare categories after the existing ones, so that every category is covered by many examples

stem: An MLflow trace of one request shows these token counts per span: system prompt 1,200; retriever result 9,800 (ten chunks, the answer used two); model call 1,000; final answer 250. The team wants to improve focus without hurting recall. Which change fits?

choices.text: Remove the retriever and let the model answer from its own knowledge, which removes the largest span
Shorten the system prompt to 300 tokens, since it is the only part of the context that the team writes by hand
Return fewer, better-ranked chunks by lowering the result count, and return only the columns the answer needs
Cap the final answer at 100 tokens so that the whole request uses less of the budget

stem: A system prompt for a travel-booking agent has 40 numbered rules. Thirty-four cover rare edge cases (lost passport, group bookings, strikes) that apply to a few percent of requests, and answers to common requests have become less consistent. Which change improves focus?

choices.text: Keep the core rules in the prompt and load the edge-case guidance on demand, only when the request matches the situation
Rewrite each of the 34 edge-case rules in capital letters so that they stand out when the situation arises
Add a rule at the top saying that the first six rules matter most and that the remaining rules apply only if they are relevant
Move all 40 rules to the end of the prompt, since models pay the most attention to the end of the context

stem: Traces for a research agent show two contributors to its high token use: each turn re-sends the full verbatim history including every earlier tool output, and the SQL tool returns complete result sets. Which two changes improve focus? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Re-send the full history every turn but sort the older tool outputs by size so the largest are read first
Raise the maximum output tokens so the agent can write longer answers that use up more of the history
Replace older tool outputs in the history with short summaries or references, and keep recent turns verbatim
Add a second SQL tool that returns the same whole result sets so the model can compare them
Make the SQL tool return aggregates or a limited, column-trimmed result rather than whole result sets

stem: An agent has two retriever tools, one over product manuals and one over support articles. For many questions both return the same chunk of text, and the trace shows the duplicate chunk appearing twice in the prompt, along with its repeated neighbors. What change improves focus?

choices.text: Increase the number of results from each retriever so the duplicates are diluted by additional passages
De-duplicate retrieved chunks before they are added to the context, so each distinct passage appears once
Ask the model in the prompt to treat repeated passages as especially reliable because they are repeated
Merge the two source indexes into a single index but keep calling both retrievers with the same query

stem: A ticket-triage agent labels each incoming message with one of six categories and extracts the order id. It handles a very high volume. Its traces show extended thinking enabled, and most output tokens of each request go to reasoning. An MLflow evaluation shows the same label accuracy with thinking turned off. Which reasoning mode should this step use?

choices.text: Extended thinking plus worked reasoning chains in the prompt, so the model writes shorter thoughts for each category
Extended thinking with a larger thinking budget, because more reasoning tokens raise accuracy on classification as well
Extended thinking with a smaller maximum output, so the visible label is cut to the shortest possible text
Standard or reduced thinking, because a simple and well-specified task gains nothing from extra reasoning tokens

stem: A nightly agent builds crew shift schedules under many interacting constraints (rest periods, certifications, shift swaps). With the standard mode its short answers often violate one or more constraints, as judged by an MLflow scorer. The job runs overnight, so latency does not matter, and the team has token budget to spare. Which choice fits?

choices.text: Use extended thinking for the planning call with a budget sized for the constraint checks
Use reduced thinking and split the schedule into one call per crew member so each answer is short
Keep the standard mode and repeat the full constraint list three times in the user turn so it receives more attention
Keep the standard mode and raise the temperature so the model explores more candidate schedules in its single answer

stem: A team enables extended thinking on `databricks-claude-sonnet-4-5` through the Anthropic Messages API, with `budget_tokens` set to 8000 and `max_tokens` also set to 8000. The request is rejected, and even a request that ran would leave no room for the visible answer after the reasoning. Which change fits?

choices.text: Raise `max_tokens` above the thinking budget, leaving room for the visible answer after the reasoning tokens
Remove the thinking setting entirely and expect the same reasoning depth from the standard mode
Lower `max_tokens` further, so the model is forced to think more briefly and still answers within the limit
Write "think for 8,000 tokens" in the system prompt and leave both numeric settings unchanged

stem: A migration assistant runs three steps per request: (1) rewrite the user message into a standalone search query, (2) plan a multi-system migration with dependent actions, (3) answer a short factual follow-up from retrieved text. The team can set the reasoning mode for each step. Which two assignments fit best? (Select TWO)

choices.text: No thinking for the migration-planning step, to keep the window free for the tool outputs of the migration
Extended thinking for the query-rewriting step, because every step of a pipeline should use the deepest mode available
Reduced or no thinking for the query-rewriting step, which is short, well specified and runs on every request
Extended thinking for the short factual answer, so the model re-derives the retrieved facts before it replies
Extended thinking, or a high effort setting, for the migration-planning step, where a wrong ordering of dependent actions is costly

stem: An agent's context is 90% tool output from three verbose SQL calls, and it now answers from the wrong table. A teammate proposes switching on extended thinking so the model will "reason past" the irrelevant rows. Which response is best?

choices.text: Agree, and also have the model restate every tool output inside its thinking so that it can compare all of them
Cut the tool output first (needed columns and rows only, old outputs cleared), then add thinking only if still needed
Disagree, but double `max_tokens` so the model has plenty of space left over after reading all the tool output
Agree: deeper reasoning lets the model ignore irrelevant rows, so the large tool outputs can stay in place as they are

stem: A policy agent places 40 retrieved passages, about 70,000 tokens, in its prompt. An MLflow evaluation shows correct answers when the relevant clause is among the first or last few passages and frequent misses when it sits in the middle, although the model's window is far from full. Which change addresses this most directly?

choices.text: Raise the reasoning effort so the model reads each of the 40 passages in more depth before it answers
Move to a model with a larger window so the 40 passages fit and the middle gets equal attention
Duplicate the full passage list at the end of the prompt, so every clause appears again near the question
Keep a handful of top-ranked passages and put the most relevant one next to the question, instead of all 40

stem: To improve recall, a team raised an agent's retriever from returning 5 chunks to 25. The correct chunk now appears in the returned set in more traces, but the answer correctness score in MLflow evaluation went down, and answers often cite loosely related chunks. Which change should the team make?

choices.text: Return a small number of chunks, add a re-ranker or metadata filter to put the right chunk on top, and re-run the evaluation
Keep 25 chunks and shorten each chunk to one sentence, so the extra chunks cost fewer tokens in the window
Keep 25 chunks and tell the model in the prompt to ignore chunks that are less relevant than the correct one
Return 100 chunks, since recall in the retrieved set was the real objective and correctness will recover with more material

stem: An agent calls its AI Search tool with the entire conversation transcript as the query text. Early in a chat the retrieved chunks are on topic; after dozens of turns they drift toward unrelated subjects that appeared earlier in the chat. Which change restores retrieval quality?

choices.text: Increase the chunk overlap in the index so each chunk repeats more neighbouring text
Increase the number of results returned, so on-topic chunks will appear among the drifting ones
Switch to a larger embedding model, since a long transcript query needs a bigger vector to represent its meaning
Have the agent write a short, self-contained query for the current need and send only that to the retriever

stem: A contract-review agent receives 20 full documents in one prompt and is asked to compare their termination clauses. The answers are shallow and miss clauses from documents in the middle of the set. Which redesign best restores quality while keeping token use moderate?

choices.text: Raise the temperature so the model samples different readings of the 20 documents and picks the longest answer
Extract the termination clauses from each document in separate small calls, then compare the extracts in a final call
Keep all 20 documents and add "read every document carefully" at the start and end
Drop every other document at random, so the set is half as long and the middle gets more attention

stem: A team wants to learn at which context size its agent's accuracy starts to fall, to set a working context budget. They have an MLflow 3 evaluation dataset and scorers, and traces record token counts. Which approach gives a usable answer?

choices.text: Compare only average latency across several prompt sizes, since quality always stays flat until the whole window is full
Use the model's maximum context window as the budget, since the vendor sized it for full use
Run one evaluation at several prompt sizes, padding the same content with realistic extra context, and set the budget where scores drop
Run one evaluation with the longest possible prompt, and if it passes, use that length as the budget

stem: A curator configures a Genie Agent and sorts the knowledge to enter. Which two items belong in the agent's general text instructions rather than in another instruction type? (Select TWO)

choices.text: The definition of "active customer", a filter that almost every revenue question uses, written as a sentence
A formatting rule: if the question gives no other specification, round all decimals to two places
The meaning of one ambiguous column such as `amt_2`, entered once as a general note for the whole agent
A multi-step comparison of cohort retention that needs several joins, described in prose for Genie to copy
The company's fiscal year starts on 1 February, so "FY26" means 1 February 2026 to 31 January 2027

stem: A Genie Agent's text instructions say "round all decimals to two places", but two of its example SQL queries round to whole numbers. Users see different rounding for similar questions and the curator wants consistent answers. What should the curator do?

choices.text: Delete every example query, because text instructions are the only source Genie treats as authoritative
Copy the rounding instruction into several table descriptions, so Genie reads it more often than it reads the examples
Write the rounding instruction again in capital letters, so it overrides the two example queries
Make the types agree, by changing the two example queries to round to two places

stem: Users ask a Genie Agent broad questions such as "how is sales performance?". Genie picks a time range and a channel on its own, and the figures are not what the users had in mind. The business wants Genie to ask for the missing details instead of guessing. Which configuration achieves this?

choices.text: Add the sentence "Be careful when answering sales questions" to the general instructions
Create a SQL expression that fixes the time range to the last 30 days and the channel to online for every sales question
Add a closing general instruction: if sales performance is asked without time range, channel or KPIs, ask first, with sample wording
Hide the date and channel columns so Genie cannot choose them without being told

stem: A new Genie Agent for support operations is shared with a wide audience. Users drift to topics the agent was never set up for (HR, finance) and get weak answers. The curator wants the first screen to steer users to what the agent handles well. Which configuration fits?

choices.text: Configure sample questions for the supported tasks, phrased as users ask them and checked by the curator
Add the instruction "refuse every question that is not about support" and keep the unrelated tables in the agent
Leave sample questions empty and rely on users typing their own, because Genie answers questions on any topic equally well
Add every table of the support workspace to the agent so that any topic users raise has some data behind it

stem: A curator adds a general instruction saying to use `order_dt` for order dates. She then retests the same question in the chat where Genie had already answered wrongly several times, and the answer is still wrong. What should she do next?

choices.text: Retest in a new chat with a clean history, and if still wrong, add an example query that uses `order_dt`
Remove all text instructions and test again, since text instructions cannot influence which column is used
Restart the SQL warehouse attached to the agent, in case it holds the earlier wrong instruction in its cache
Rewrite the instruction in capital letters and add three paraphrases, so that Genie overrides the earlier wrong answers

stem: A support agent's prompt has 12 few-shot examples of about 150 tokens each. In an MLflow evaluation on a fixed dataset, correctness is 0.61 with no examples, 0.82 with three, 0.83 with six and 0.83 with twelve. Token cost matters. Which set should the team keep?

choices.text: None, since zero-shot is the cheapest configuration and examples only add cost
All twelve, since every added example scored at least as high as before
Six examples that are most similar to each other, so the output format is reinforced more strongly in every response
The three examples that produced the main gain, dropping the others whose marginal contribution is close to zero

stem: A returns-handling agent's prompt holds five few-shot examples, all clear-cut cases. Traces show it still fails on ambiguous requests, such as a refund request that is really an exchange. The team can add roughly the same number of example tokens. Which change is best?

choices.text: Replace the examples with full multi-turn conversations, so the model sees more context per example
Replace some examples with ones on the confusing boundary (refund versus exchange), showing the correct handling of each
Add ten more clear-cut examples of the same kind, since more examples of correct behavior generalize to ambiguous cases
Remove the examples and add a paragraph describing ambiguous cases, twice as long as the old examples

stem: A team keeps 10 few-shot examples in an extraction agent's prompt and must cut tokens without losing quality. It has an MLflow 3 evaluation dataset with scorers, and traces record the token count of every request. Which two steps let it decide which examples to keep? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Run the evaluation once with all 10 examples and drop the ones whose inputs look least like the dataset
Keep the examples with the most tokens, since long examples carry the most information per example
Re-run the same evaluation with each example removed in turn, and drop those whose removal leaves scores unchanged
Ask the model which examples it finds most useful, and drop those it ranks lowest in its own answer
Compare the score against the number of examples in several runs, and read per-request token cost from the traces

stem: A classification agent has 200 labeled examples across 15 intents, far too many for the prompt. A fixed set of five examples helps only some intents. The team wants help for every intent at a fixed token budget per request. Which design fits?

choices.text: Index the examples in AI Search and per request add only the few most similar to the incoming message
Put all 200 examples into an agent memory store and inject the store into the system prompt
Put all 200 examples in the prompt once and rely on the model's window to hold them for the whole conversation
Pick five examples at random for each request, so that over many requests every intent is shown to the model

stem: An email-drafting agent's prompt has three examples that all mention a customer called "Acme" and a refund of $45. Production outputs for unrelated customers keep mentioning Acme or $45. Which change corrects this?

choices.text: Move the three examples from the system prompt into the user turn, so the model treats them as the real request each time
Add "do not copy the examples" in capitals and keep the three examples exactly as they are
Vary names and amounts across examples, with marked placeholders for details that must not carry over
Repeat the same three examples twice more, so the format is learned strongly enough to stop the copying

stem: A 2,000-token system prompt works well except for refund questions, which are a few percent of requests: traces show the agent skipping the identity check that must precede any refund. The team wants the cheapest fix that is easy to maintain. Which is best?

choices.text: Rewrite the whole prompt from scratch with a new structure, so that all rules receive equal weight again, including refunds
Add one short, specific rule: before any refund, verify the customer's identity, and say which tool to call first
Paste the full 1,500-word refund policy into the prompt, so the agent has every detail at hand
Add ten worked refund examples at the end of the prompt, covering every refund situation in the policy

stem: A system prompt includes the line "Format dates correctly." Traces show the agent writing dates in several formats, which breaks a downstream parser. The team wants the fix that adds the fewest tokens. Which revision is best?

choices.text: Add three full sample dialogues in which every date is written correctly
Repeat "Format dates correctly" in capitals at the start, middle and end of the prompt
Keep the line and add an explanatory paragraph on why consistent dates matter to the downstream parser and reports
Replace it with a specific rule: "Write dates as YYYY-MM-DD, for example 2026-11-09"

stem: After six incremental patches, a system prompt has overlapping rules and several "never do X" lines, and each new patch seems to break a different behavior. Which prompt-revision strategy is best?

choices.text: Freeze the prompt and cover the new failures by raising the reasoning effort for every request
Consolidate: merge overlapping rules, drop rules the traces show never matter, then re-run the same evaluation
Split the prompt into two system prompts and alternate between them on odd and even turns of the whole conversation
Keep appending each new fix at the end of the prompt, since the last lines are read most reliably

stem: Traces show an agent passing relative dates such as "next Friday" to its `get_shipments(ship_date STRING)` tool, which expects `YYYY-MM-DD`; the tool then fails. The team wants the lowest token cost and the easiest maintenance. Which two revisions fit? (Select TWO)

choices.text: Add five complete sample dialogues of correct tool calls to the system prompt, covering every date phrasing users have used
Turn on extended thinking for every request, so the model works out the format before each call
Copy the whole function signature and return schema into the system prompt as a second full description of the tool
Make the tool's failure message state the expected format and one valid example, so the agent corrects the call on a retry
Add a one-line rule to the system prompt: convert dates to `YYYY-MM-DD` before calling `get_shipments`, for example `2026-11-13`

stem: One agent serves 30 tenants. Each tenant has a few special rules, and the team currently keeps one growing system prompt with "if tenant is X" branches. The prompt is long, edits for one tenant have broken others, and every request carries rules for 29 tenants it does not need. Which revision fits best?

choices.text: Keep a short shared core prompt and insert only the current tenant's rules into it at request time
Keep all 30 tenants' branches in one prompt, but move them to the end so the model reads them last
Remove the tenant rules and let extended thinking infer what each tenant probably wants from the user's wording and tone
Make a full copy of the whole system prompt for each tenant and edit each copy separately
